title: Open just three hours a day, a new Tokyo soba joint serves up wildly addictive regional noodles
description: No need to travel up north for these thick, chewy noodles, but you’ll have to adapt your lunch schedule to match theirs. With ramen chains like Ichiran taking up a lot of social media screen time, it’s no wonder that ramen is one of Japan’s must-eat foods, but other noodle dishes throughout Japan hold just […]
content:
No need to travel up north for these thick, chewy noodles, but you’ll have to adapt your lunch schedule to match theirs.

With ramen chains like Ichiran taking up a lot of social media screen time, it’s no wonder that ramen is one of Japan’s must-eat foods, but other noodle dishes throughout Japan hold just as much importance in the country’s culinary scene, perhaps even more given their longer history, impact on culture, and more refined appeal. Buckwheat noodles, known as soba, are one such dish, having hundreds of years to work into the hearts and stomachs of Japan’s populace, culminating in several regional variations that are all equally a delight to enjoy.

Our Japanese-language reporter P.K. Sanjun recently had his first experience with Yamagata soba, and was instantly addicted. The dark-colored, thick soba was extraordinarily filling and hearty, making for an insanely delicious bowl. However, he must admit that he needs to apologize to any geographic loyalists out there, as his first ever Yamagata soba was actually eaten in Sendai, Miyagi (its neighboring prefecture).

As he thought back on that bowl of heaven, P.K. couldn’t help but wonder if it were possible to eat Yamagata soba in Tokyo too, and after doing some research, he discovered that the very shop he ate at in Sendai had opened its first Tokyo branch this year. Truly, this must be the work of the noodle gods calling him forth to fulfil his destiny.

The name of the shop P.K. ate at in Sendai was Nikusoba Toshichi, and just as it suggests, the specialty of the shop is ‘nikusoba’ (literally ‘meat soba’). The meat in question is chicken, but more specifically chickens that have finished laying eggs, which are known as oyadori and have a deep umami and firm texture, and the broth is also apparently made from chicken.

▼ Nikusoba Toshichi’s Sendai branch

However, P.K. had a lingering regret: the original specialty of the store is cold nikusoba, but Sendai on that day was terrifyingly cold, so the staff recommended the warm nikusoba instead.

▼ Warm nikusoba

It was tremendously delicious, but he just couldn’t get over his desire to try it cold, so with the arrival of Nikusoba Toshichi’s expansion into central Tokyo, his chance for a redo arrived a lot sooner than he had anticipated.

Located roughly between the Tokyo Metro’s Hanzomon and Nagatacho Subway Stations, a stone’s throw from the Imperial Palace, the new store was very conveniently situated. Business hours are the same three hours as in Sendai, 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m., and since it’s closed on Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays, your only option is to go on a weekday—which seems to be a power play by the store that says, “adjust your life to our noodle schedule, not the other way around.”

Even so… Nikusoba Toshichi is worth it a hundred times over. After walking about five minutes from Hanzomon Station, P.K. arrived at the Hanzomon Branch and was greeted by a line of about ten people that had formed in front of the shop.

Just like in the Sendai store, there was plenty of standing-room eating space, so the turnover is a lot faster than might be expected, meaning that P.K. only had about 15 minutes to wait before his turn arrived.

P.K. ordered the Nikusoba Large Serving (1,050 yen [US$6.57], and topped it with gesoten (deep-fried squid tentacle tempura, a beloved regional pairing in Yamagata) for an additional 250 yen. What he hadn’t realized was that the large serving has an incredible 600 grams (about 1.3 pounds) of soba, and the even larger ‘dekkai’ size has 800 grams (nearly 1.8 pounds).

Shortly after ordering, the nikusoba arrived, characterized by its clear golden-hued soup and dark, thick soba. Taking a sip of the soup, it’s a sweet taste and a temperature that isn’t ice-cold as you might expect, but rather around ‘lukewarm’.

The soba has the chewiness it looks like it would have—the type you savor by chewing rather than for how smoothly it goes down the throat. This soba, ground from the buckwheat seed together with its inner husk, is in stark contrast to the thin, white noodles you’ll often see at other places in Tokyo.

The chicken also has a firm, dense texture, and the more you chew it, the more the flavor comes out.

The richly seasoned gesoten complemented the rest of the dish so well, P.K. couldn’t imagine ever having the dish without it as a topping.

Soba tends to carry a refined, elegant image in Japan, yet the chewiness and bursting flavors of Toshichi’s nikusoba was a bowl that was endlessly wild.

Being open for only three hours on weekdays is a high hurdle to clear for a lot of people, but even so, having a place where you can eat nikusoba without going all the way to Sendai is something to be grateful for. Yamagata soba is a wild soba hiding tremendous potential, so if you find yourself in Tokyo on a weekday around lunchtime, loosen your belt, and go conquer a mountain of glorious, chewy buckwheat.

title: Krispy Kreme Japan has a new Year of the Ram donut and one more lucky New Year’s treat
description: Edible eto. Sometimes, Japanese can be a wonderfully concise language. For example, when talking about the representative animals for each year in traditional Asian divination, in English you’d need to say “Chinese Zodiac animals.” In Japanese, though, you can get the same job done with just two syllables, since the members of that zoological Zodiac […]
content:
Edible eto.

Sometimes, Japanese can be a wonderfully concise language. For example, when talking about the representative animals for each year in traditional Asian divination, in English you’d need to say “Chinese Zodiac animals.” In Japanese, though, you can get the same job done with just two syllables, since the members of that zoological Zodiac set are called eto.

Now, maybe you don’t find yourself discussing the Chinese Zodiac animals all that often, but when an occasion does arise in which you need to tell people something about them as quickly as possible, eto is a word you’ll be glad to know. For instance, right now we need to tell you that Krispy Kreme Japan has a new eto donut on the way!

The donut chain has just revealed its new Hitsuji Vanilla Cream donut, with hitusji being the Japanese word for both ram and sheep (told you it can be a concise language). This adorable treat has a white chocolate coating, but while it might look fluffy, it’s actually going to have a lot of crunch to it. In addition to the white chocolate crunch sprinkled across it, it has hazelnuts for the tuft of “wool” on its forehead, and chocolate pieces for the ears, eyes, and mouth. Waiting inside the donut is a sweet milky vanilla cream filling.

Unlike most other parts of Asia, Japan changes over to the new eto animal on January 1, so the Hitsuji Vanilla Cream is going to be going on sale in late December, on the 26th, to be precise. The Year of the Ram dessert will be joined from the same day by another New Year’s-themed donut, the Lucky Strawberry.

Red and white are the traditional New Year’s colors in Japan, seen as an auspicious combination full of fortuitous portents for the months to come. That might seem a bit lofty in terms of ambitions for a donut, but strawberry fans will no doubt feel like things are going their way as they bite into the white chocolate-covered coating with a strawberry nappage glaze. The sprinkling of freeze-dried strawberry bits where the two lines of white chocolate meet are meant to conjure up thoughts of a mizuhiki, the coiled cord decorations customarily put up for New Year’s in Japan.

The Hitsuji Vanilla Cream is priced at 440 yen (US$2.75) and the Lucky Strawberry at 341 yen, and they’re both scheduled to be on sale until January 12. For that same availability period (December 26-January 12), they can also be purchased as part of an Eto Dozen (3,300 yen), Eto Half-dozen (1,804 yen), or three-donut Eto Box (1,144 yen), accompanied by assortments of other Krispy Kreme donuts, including the chocolate-cream filled Chocolate Snowman with its strawberry-glaze scarf.

Oh, and don’t worry, the 396-yen Chocolate Snowman will also be available to spend Christmas with you, as it goes on sale December 1.

title: Bus driver fired for licking inside of the bus during livestream
description: He’s going to have problems in his next job interviews. Being a bus driver is a difficult job, and having to get a massive vehicle through the often tight and packed streets of Japan every day is bound to take a mental toll. It’s enough to make someone want to just let go and lick […]
content:
He’s going to have problems in his next job interviews.

Being a bus driver is a difficult job, and having to get a massive vehicle through the often tight and packed streets of Japan every day is bound to take a mental toll. It’s enough to make someone want to just let go and lick the interior of public transportation. Well, it’s enough with the help of a livestreamer egging them on at least.

That’s what happened according to Keikyu Bus and the many people who watched it live online. On 16 November, an unidentified bus driver appeared on a livestream of a young woman named Riakyun and was asked by her to lick the handrail and hand strap of his bus after it went out of service for the day.

Video and images of it began to circulate on social media, causing the driver to apparently see the saliva-coated writing on the wall and report himself to his employers at Keikyu Bus. On 18 November, Keikyu issued a public apology and promised to take the appropriate actions. Then, on 20 November, they announced that the bus in question had been identified and thoroughly disinfected, and that the driver had been relieved of his duties.

Meanwhile, readers of the news online largely felt that Mother Nature has some further penalties in store for this driver. They’re likely right too. Studies have shown that he’d have been taking less of a risk licking a public toilet seat than a public railing.

“Wouldn’t you catch the flu from doing that?”
“Just, wow…”
“Seeing it was even grosser than I imagined.”
“Why are people watching this?”
“Is he trying to build up his immune system?”
“Maybe he’s replenishing his salt intake.”
“I’m more worried about that guy’s health than grossed out.”
“He’s like a yokai.”
“I wouldn’t even touch those things with my hand.”
“He clearly loves buses. Give him a raise!”
“The woman told him to do it, though.”

I don’t think Keikyu Bus has the authority to fire the streamer. They probably could file some sort of lawsuit for the cost of cleaning, but I imagine they’d rather just put this all behind them as soon as possible. They also promised to thoroughly train and instruct all drivers to prevent this from happening again.

So, let us take a moment to send our thoughts and prayers to the biggest victims of this incident: all the other bus drivers who now have to attend a seminar telling them not to lick the inside of their buses.

title: Hello Kitty would like to be squeezed between your thighs in her new plushie form [Pics]
description: Why hello, Kitty-chan. We didn’t expect to see you there. content:
Why hello, Kitty-chan. We didn’t expect to see you there.

Hello Kitty’s legendarily strong work ethic and broad range of interests mean that she can show up in some very unexpected places. On the side of a 100-meter (328-foot) tall Ferris wheel? Yep. On toilet paper with a sweet aroma? Yeah, she can be there this afternoon.

And now, squeezed between your thighs? Sure, not a problem.

Of course, this specialized purpose requires a special Hello Kitty, which is why the Sanrio star, and some of her closest friends, are joining the Mugyuuus lineup. Mugyu is a Japanese onomatopoeia for something squeezable, and Mugyuuus is a brand of weighted plushies from Japanese lifestyle goods maker Dreams.

With a weight of 420 grams (14.8-ounce), the Sanrio Mugyuuus are designed to be held between your legs while you’re sitting at a desk for an extended period of time, such as when you’re working, studying, or reading SoraNews24. The plushies aren’t so heavy that you’ll have to exert crushing force on them, but they’ll still require a bit of pressure to keep from sliding down to the floor. Dreams says they help build strength in your adductor and pelvic floor muscles, and also promote good posture and help prevent bow-leggedness and pelvic misalignment by discouraging you from crossing your legs or leaning laterally.

In addition to Kitty-chan, Cinnamoroll, My Melody, Kuromi, Pompompurin, and Pochacco are also getting Mugyuuu makeovers.

Dreams says that when you look down and you and your special Sanrio friend’s eyes meet, the cuteness will give you an extra burst of energy to help you power through tough work or school assignments, but it seems like that might be tempered with some awkwardness until you get used to their presence down there.

Each Sanrio Mugyuuu is priced at 3,300 yen (US$21), and the whole batch goes on sale November 26, with preorders placeable through the Dreams online store here.

title: Has a Shibuya restaurant solved the problem of one of Japan’s most divisive soba noodle toppings?
description: Soba-loving Seiji finds something that people who love croquette soba will love, and people who hate croquette soba might love it too. Pretty much everyone in Japan likes soba noodles, and pretty much everyone in Japan likes croquettes too. Sure, some people like them more than others do, but it’d be tough to find someone […]
content:
Soba-loving Seiji finds something that people who love croquette soba will love, and people who hate croquette soba might love it too.

Pretty much everyone in Japan likes soba noodles, and pretty much everyone in Japan likes croquettes too. Sure, some people like them more than others do, but it’d be tough to find someone who flat-out dislikes either one of the broadly-loved staples.

However, while soba and croquettes are both widely well-liked, opinions get much more divided when you start talking about eating a croquette and soba noodles together.

On the surface, it seems like using a croquette as a soba topping shouldn’t ruffle anyone’s feathers. After all, if noodles and mixed tempura work perfectly fine with soba broth, why not a croquette, which is still within the same broad category of fried starchiness?

The problem, according to the anti-croquette soba camp, is that the flavors don’t mesh well. Soba broth is made from dashi (bonito stock) and soy sauce, an unmistakably classical Japanese flavor profile. Croquettes, on the other hand, come from Western cuisine, so while they’re often enjoyed with a similarly occidentally inspired Worcester-like sauce, letting a croquette soak in soba broth leads to a discordant result in which east doesn’t meet west so much as the two culinary traditions stare awkwardly at each other from across the room.

Taking all that into account, our Japanese-language reporter Seiji Nakazawa can very much understand why some people don’t like croquette soba, but he has no personal problem with it. So when he recently stopped into a branch of soba chain Shibua Soba in Tokyo’s Shibuya neighborhood and saw that they had croquette soba on the menu, he decided to order it, thinking it might give him something to recommend to fellow croquette soba fans.

To his surprise, it ended up giving him something to recommend to croquette soba haters too.

Why? Because that’s not just any regular old croquette he ordered…

…but a saba (mackerel) croquette!

Fish croquettes are pretty rare in Japan, but they’re a specialty of the town of Hidaka in Wakayama Prefecture. Wakayama is also famous for its ume (Japanese plum), and so Hidaka-style mackerel croquettes are made by marinating the fish in plum vinegar, then mixing it in with the mashed potato and deep-frying them.

This gives the mackerel croquette a much more traditional Japanese taste than a typical all-potato one, and that, in turn, helps bridge the gap between it and the soba broth. Again, Seiji likes croquette soba with orthodox croquettes too, but this mackerel croquette makes for an extremely harmonious combination, especially if you leave it in the broth long enough for the liquid to soak all the way through to its core.

You end up with something that will still totally satisfy croquette soba fans, but which also addresses the major complaint from people who don’t like croquette soba. Seiji is confident that whichever side of the debate someone usually finds themselves on, they’ll love this dish, and it has him wondering whether there might also be ways in the world to find common ground on other decisive topics, such as whether cats or dogs make the better pet, or whether chocolate snacks shaped like mushrooms or bamboo shoots are the superior sweet treat.

Currently, though, the mackerel croquette soba, as well as its udon noodle sibling, are available only at the Shibuya Dogenzaka branch of Shibu Soba, where they’re priced at 650 yen (US$4.10). Considering how, in Seiji’s estimation, this has the potential to be a hit with 100 percent of the people in Japan, though, hopefully it’ll spread to other locations in the chain soon.

title: Make Gifu’s famous autumn chestnut sweet at home with just two Japanese supermarket snacks
description: No peeling or boiling required in this super-easy zero-cook recipe. Japan has an abundance of seasonal foods, giving residents reasons to constantly look forward to the coming of the next season. I first noticed when trying to hunt down fresh strawberries and pears during the summer, only to be left shocked by the complete lack […]
content:
No peeling or boiling required in this super-easy zero-cook recipe.

Japan has an abundance of seasonal foods, giving residents reasons to constantly look forward to the coming of the next season. I first noticed when trying to hunt down fresh strawberries and pears during the summer, only to be left shocked by the complete lack of availability in my local few supermarkets. This is not a phenomenon limited to fruit, as certain vegetables, mushrooms, and even full dishes see their supplies fluctuate throughout the year. The moment autumn arrives in Japan, many Japanese people start to crave chestnuts, and our Japanese-language reporter Natsuno Futon isn’t any different. In fact, being from Gifu, a certain chestnut-based wagashi (traditional Japanese sweet) holds a very nostalgic place in her heart: kurikinton.

Kurikinton has a common form and a more regional form: the common is a glossy, bright yellow sweet potato and candied chestnut paste typically served as part of Japanese New Year’s dishes, but the regional Gifu version is a traditional tea confection made simply by mashing boiled chestnuts with sugar and shaping them into mounds.

The season for kurikinton is almost over, and yet Natsuno found herself longing for that soft, crumbly treat, debating whether or not to order some from a specialty shop, such as Kawakamiya or Suya, both based in Nakatsugawa. However, to Natsuno, kurikinton was always something her mother made at home rather than being something bought at a store, so one day as she was strolling through the shopping aisles, she stopped in her tracks when she spotted a certain product.

While Natsuno would generally opt to buy raw chestnuts and make kurikinton from scratch, she decided to see if she could substitute something ready-made for it instead, but first she needed to get the recipe from her mother.

Natsuno’s mother is a talker, and it took 15 minutes of her discussing her latest purchase of a Legoland Japan annual pass and her recent cafe breakfast to finally get around to talking about kurikinton. Her mother explained that as the chestnuts grown at Natsuno’s grandmother’s house weren’t particularly flavorful on their own, her mother used to add sweet potatoes and sugar to boost the sweetness.

With this pretty rough explanation and a vague memory of having watched her mother make it before, Natsuno was fairly confident she would be able to pull it off. She prepared two bags of Maruyanagi’s Whole Peeled Moist Sweet Chestnuts and one bag of Bite-Sized Sweet Potatoes, all costing 214 yen (US$1.34) each.

Since both were already cooked, there was zero hassle of peeling or boiling, and being already sweetened too, Natsuno skipped out on adding any extra sugar or seasonings. While her mother told her that adding just a tiny bit of sweet potato would be fine, it felt awkward to have leftovers, so she just decided to use everything.

After lightly patting off the moisture with paper towels, Natsuno tossed them into a food processor, although it’s just as simple to mash them by hand.

Next, the mixture was transferred to a bowl and mashed together so it would hold its shape.

When just a few small chestnut chunks remained, Natsuno stopped mixing it together, ending up with a texture that was neither too dry and crumbly nor too sticky and gooey.

Once all mixed up, all that was left was to wrap about 40 grams (1.4 ounces) in plastic wrap and twist the top, and while her mother used to fasten it with something like a twist tie or pipe cleaner, Natsuno didn’t have any to hand, so substituted with washi tape.

The recipe is complete, making for a total of seven pieces, and while the appearances looked pretty respectable the key lay in the taste.

▼ “Yes! Yes! This is it!”

Natsuno’s makeshift recipe made for a decent kurikinton, with both the moist, dense texture and the bits of chestnut left throughout being just as she had imagined them to be. The sweetness was also just right, and it was well-received by Natsuno’s children too. However, one thing she did notice was that the packaged chestnuts and sweet potatoes she used contained brown sugar, which made the flavor slightly different from the standard Gifu kurikinton. If she thought of it as a brown sugar-flavored kurikinton, it was perfectly delicious.

Although, there was one thing that Natsuno couldn’t help but be curious about in that, being from Gifu, she was no doubt looking at kurikinton through nostalgia-tinted glasses, so she wanted to find out how someone who had never eaten the regional style of kurikinton would feel about her creation. Upon having a friend sample it, Natsuno’s kurikinton received high praise, so she was pleased to know that the recipe worked.

Any leftovers can be put into a storage bag and frozen, and Natsuno recommends trying them half-thawed as she used to relish in doing when she was a kid.

While the authentic kurikinton season is almost over, it’s easy to make this with everyday supermarket ingredients, and if you fall in love with it, be sure to pay a visit to Gifu when you’re in the area.

title: 4-cheese-pizza-flavored soda unleashed on Japan [Taste Test]
description: It’s disgustingly delicious! It’s probably a sign of current economic hardships facing the world, but in Japan there has been a significant shortage of wacky flavor concepts in recent years. It stands to reason as companies tighten their purse strings and refrain from excessive R&D, while customers are spending their increasingly hard-earned money on more […]
content:
It’s disgustingly delicious!

It’s probably a sign of current economic hardships facing the world, but in Japan there has been a significant shortage of wacky flavor concepts in recent years. It stands to reason as companies tighten their purse strings and refrain from excessive R&D, while customers are spending their increasingly hard-earned money on more reliable products.

But one company still carrying the torch of kookiness is Cheerio, a Kyoto-based beverage maker and vending machine operator that has made a name for itself with bold ideas over the years. They’ve served up drinks disguised as soy sauce and mayonnaise and invented a soda flavored as caramel popcorn. They’ve even sold bottled hot water, which doesn’t sound so crazy but is something hardly ever done.

Now, Cheerio is back with perhaps their most fearsome flavor yet: 4-cheese-pizza-flavored soda. Officially called Quattro Formaggi Flavor Soda, it sets out to mimic the pungent aroma and creamy sweetness of a cheesy pizza in a carbonated beverage. Naturally, there was a fair bit of online buzz about it.

“That’s a rare one. I’m definitely going to hunt it down.”
“I tried it as soon as I could. Their development team is incredible!”
“Cheerio’s done it again… I need to find this.”
“This will never be a permanent flavor, but it’s an amazing pinch hitter.”
“Uh… I’m good, thanks.”
“If I drank this while I had a cold, I’d probably puke.”
“If they went to the trouble of making it and selling it, it can’t possibly be bad, can it?”

That last commenter is either too young to remember or has forgotten the spaghetti-flavored ice candy disaster of 2014. Still, I held out a little hope for this unusual flavor, mainly because I’m a huge fan of the sadly discontinued kimchi-flavored soda.

By name alone, that might sound like an especially rank-tasting concoction, but its charm lay in its secret weapon of a flavor: garlic. That little bulbous plant is a key bridge between the sweet and savory notes of a kimchi-flavored soda, making it not just a successful novelty flavor, but one of the best I’ve ever had.

So, it was with a very open mind that I went out and bought a bottle from a nearby Cheerio vending machine. It cost 120 yen (US$0.75) and was slightly smaller than most bottled sodas, at only 350 milliliters (12 ounces), but depending how this pans out, that could be a good thing.

Quattro Formaggi Flavor Soda let its presence be known immediately after twisting off the cap. An invisible cloud of pure cheese odor seemed to violently erupt from the bottle neck. To Cheerio’s credit, the smell of blended cheeses was amazingly accurate. According to the website, the four cheese flavors are cheddar, Gouda, cream cheese, and Gorgonzola.

▼ Despite the bottle’s label, there is no Swiss cheese involved. A little honey flavor was added as well, just like the real pizza often has.

Upon first swig, my initial reaction was, “Sweet Jesus, this is nasty!” And yet, oddly, at the same time it was kind of good. I’m a huge fan of pizza in all its forms, and this definitely tasted like a quattro formaggi. It’s just the fact that it was liquid made it particularly unsettling. It tasted just like real cheese… cold, wet, and bubbly cheese.

No half-steps were taken here. The cheese flavor was authentic and overwhelming. However, the aftertaste also had no intention of leaving my mouth any time soon, so I could savor the great taste of gorgonzola throughout the day, the natto-like notes in particular. I can only imagine the toll it took on my breath as well and don’t recommend this before any important business meetings. Perhaps if they harnessed the awesome power of garlic like kimchi soda had, it would have been a more enjoyable drink.

It’s a strange combination of being both disgusting and delicious at the same time. I’m not sure I can recommend it, but I still applaud Cheerio for the effort during this dire period for adventures in flavor. For anyone who dares try a bottle, they can be found in supermarkets and convenience stores all over Japan and in vending machines in the Kansai, Chubu, and Okinawa regions.

title: Instant curry blessed by priests at shrine of god of learning go on sale in Japan
description: Medium spiciness and good luck, both in one convenient package from Yamaguchi. Benjamin Franklin is often erroneously quoted as saying that beer is proof that God loves us and wants us to be happy. It was actually wine that he was expressing his appreciation for, but I suppose you could apply the saying to anything […]
content:
Medium spiciness and good luck, both in one convenient package from Yamaguchi.

Benjamin Franklin is often erroneously quoted as saying that beer is proof that God loves us and wants us to be happy. It was actually wine that he was expressing his appreciation for, but I suppose you could apply the saying to anything so delicious that it tastes like a gift from heaven, like, for instance, curry.

And it would be especially appropriate to see Hofu Tenmangu Tenjin Curry as a sign that divine forces want you to be happy, because it’s actually been blessed by Shinto priests.

Hofu is a town in Yamaguchi Prefecture, and its most famous feature is Hofu Tenmangu, a Shinto shrine that was established all the way back in the year 904. Enshrined within is the spirit of Sugawara no Michizane, a 9th century scholar who became deified as the god of learning, acquiring the alternate name Tenjin in the process. Hofu Tenmangu has since become a popular site for students, test-takers, and other people pursuing academic ambitions to visit and pray for success.

Less famously, Hofu is also home to HFD Foods, which specializes in freeze-dried soups. HFD’s parent company, Hachi, also makes instant curry, and so HFD wanted to whip up a new variety of its own, which it developed with feedback from taste testings held at Hofu Tenmangu and Hofy city hall. The result is Hofu Tenmangu Tenjin Curry, which boasts a mixture of over 20 spices, diced vegetables, ground beef, a sauce made from four kinds of mushrooms, and red wine.

As a symbol of local pride, a photo of Hofu Tenmangu appears on the box, and on November 6, a ceremony was held at the shrine in which priests blessed the initial batch of Hofu Tenmangu Tenjin Curry.

“This curry is made with our wishes of success for everyone who is challenging themselves, and through this ceremony, we pray that their efforts will lead to success” says Hachi.

Hofu Tenmangu Tenjin Curry goes on sale December 4, but orders can already be placed through the Hachi online store, with single packs priced at 400 yen (US2.50) here and five-packs for 1,900 yen here. With a shelf life of two years from its packaging date, having a few packets in your pantry would definitely be handy if you’re grinding away getting ready for an upcoming test and don’t have time to cook. Note, though, that it’s not clear if all packs will be blessed or just the first batch, so those looking for the maximum good-luck effect might want to put their order in sooner rather than later.

title: Yoshinoya’s 2027 lucky box is already here and brings the newest piece of mini Yoshinoya-ware
description: The newest miniature rice bowl from Yoshinoya has our otaku reporter thinking of One Piece. As regular readers of SoraNews24 will know, shops and restaurants in Japan offer “lucky bags” as part of their New Year’s celebrations, stuffing them with merch and coupons worth more than the price they charge for the bundle, and sometimes […]
content:
The newest miniature rice bowl from Yoshinoya has our otaku reporter thinking of One Piece.

As regular readers of SoraNews24 will know, shops and restaurants in Japan offer “lucky bags” as part of their New Year’s celebrations, stuffing them with merch and coupons worth more than the price they charge for the bundle, and sometimes including exclusive items you can’t get any other way. Yoshinoya is no exception, but there are two things that make their lucky bag special. First, it’s actually a lucky box, and second, you don’t have to wait until the new year to get it.

Yoshinoya’s lucky box, or fukubako, as it’s called in Japanese, went on sale through the chain’s online store on November 12. Our Japanese-language reporter Seiji Nakazawa buys one every year, both because beef bowls make up a major part of his regular diet, and also so he can get his hands on the special dishware that comes as part of the bundle along with packs of Yoshinoya toppings to pour over a bowl of white rice.

Every year, Yoshinoya has three tiers of lucky boxes, which it designates using the old-school Japanese rankings of “plum,” “bamboo,” and “pine.” Of those three, “pine” is the most premium, and this year’s 8,532-yen (US$54) pine-class lucky box comes with six pouches of beef bowl toppings, four pork bowl pouches, two packs of ginger pork, two packs of oyako (chicken and egg), one pack of fried chicken, and one pack of beef tongue.

Also part of the pine box: this crazy-looking beef bowl blanket, which can be folded up into its “bowl” when you’re not using it.

Regardless of which lucky box you order, though, the first 5,000 boxes ship with this year’s tableware, a miniature Yoshinoya bowl!

The beef bowl blanket definitely caught Seiji’s eye, but to tell the truth, he’s pretty much good for blankets right now, since he’s already got an array of them featuring his favorite anime characters. Because of that, he opted for the more moderately priced 4,320-yen “plum” lucky box, with two pouches each of toppings for beef bowls, pork bowls, and oyako bowls, plus two servings of teppan-grilled beef…

…plus the mini bowl!

Size-wise, this is arguably closer to a large sake cup than a small rice bowl. There’s no mistaking the traditional Yoshinoya logo and patterns on the outer surface…

…and the inside is marked with a kanji character for sheep/ram, a salute to the upcoming Chinese Zodiac animal that helps connect the bowl to the New Year’s/lucky bag custom.

Seiji’s been making a point of buying the Yoshinoya lucky box every year since 2020, so he’s now built up a sizable collection of the tableware pieces.

Yoshinoya could have gone the easy route and kept packing the same bowl in every year, just with a different kanji for that year’s animal. Instead, though, they’ve included a unique piece every year, including a nice chunky tea cup one time and a very avant-garde lip design for one of the bowls.

Lining them up all together, those who are sticklers for uniform order might feel a little irritated, but Seiji’s take is the complete opposite. To him, they look like the cast of One Piece, each with their own distinct idiosyncrasies, but still holding a connection to a common core that unites them.

▼ Seiji’s Yoshinoya lucky box nakama

With only the first 5,000 orders getting this year’s mini bowl, the stock won’t last long, but if you’re looking to pick up a Yoshinoya lucky box for yourself, they can be ordered through the chain’s online shop here.

title: Is Starbucks Japan’s new Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino really like a Christmas tree?
description: Green tea is designed to mimic a green tree in this latest limited-edition creation.  With Christmas now just over a month away, Starbucks is ramping up the holiday vibe with a brand new duo of festive drinks, and the star is the Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino, which has been designed to look like a Christmas tree. […]
content:
Green tea is designed to mimic a green tree in this latest limited-edition creation. 

With Christmas now just over a month away, Starbucks is ramping up the holiday vibe with a brand new duo of festive drinks, and the star is the Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino, which has been designed to look like a Christmas tree. Released on 20 November, our reporter K. Masami was first in line to try the new drinks, ordering both the Frappuccino and the equally alluring Tiramisu Latte, which are both only available for a limited time.

The Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino (720 yen [US$4.50] for dine-in) was the drink she was most curious about, as she wanted to see what made it different from the chain’s Matcha Cream Frappuccino, a standard menu item. From the outset, it looked like a richer drink, with generous amounts of whipped cream and matcha sauce at the bottom, and a top layer of mascarpone cream and matcha powder.

Taking a sip, Masami was expecting to get a strong hit of matcha, but instead she was surprised to taste the deliciousness of mascarpone cream. It instantly called to mind the flavour of tiramisu, working with the green tea to recreate the dessert with a very Japanese twist. Although the mascarpone was delicious, it was also wonderfully mellow, with a smooth, rich texture that allowed the matcha flavour to shine through.

As she worked her way through the drink, she found that it was quite similar to a Matcha Cream Frappuccino, but it was slightly less sweet, with the mascarpone cream taking some of the edge off the matcha. The result was a wonderfully rich beverage with a distinct dessert quality that sets it apart from a standard matcha drink.

As for whether it was the taste of Christmas, well it did have enough green to make you think of a Christmas tree, and the flavour was rich, like a decadent dessert you might treat yourself to during the holiday season. So in that sense, it did have a festive flair to it, but with a dash of matcha flavour that made it very Japanese.

▼ Those looking to treat themselves with something other than matcha this Christmas can opt for the Tiramisu Latte (630 yen for dine-in).

This winter warmer contains a shot of espresso, blended with hot milk and mocha-flavoured syrup, and finished with a layer of mascarpone cream and dark chocolate powder. Sipping on this was a luxurious experience, as the mascarpone added a thick and creamy richness to the familiar taste of a White Mocha, which usually contains whipped cream.

Though the mascarpone layer was delicious on its own, when mixed with the coffee base it brought the entire drink to life, making Masami sigh with content. The dusting of chocolate powder on top added a subtle bitterness that gave the latte a lovely balance, creating another indulgent drink.

▼ If you want to add some more indulgence to the festivities, there’s a new rich matcha tart (580 yen), also released on 20 November.

Rich really is the keyword here, as the matcha flavour is deep and intense, with the cream giving it a thick and satisfyingly dense texture to make matcha lovers swoon.

All these new releases are perfectly suited to winter, with a premium feel that offers an escape from the everyday as the festive season approaches. Starbucks has always been good at capturing the seasonal vibe, and these are just the thing to enjoy slowly in a cosy, warm cafe while watching the world outside gradually prepare for winter.

title: Final Fantasy/Dragon Quest Christmas trees go up as Chocobo and Slime celebrate holidays in Japan
description: Ho-ho-ho, Chocobo! It’s time for a merry Slime-mas in Yokohama. We’ve still got about a month left until Santa makes his delivery run, but some other beloved icons have already arrived and started spreading Christmas cheer in Japan. Chocobo and Slime, the mascots of Square Enix’s Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest video game franchises, are […]
content:
Ho-ho-ho, Chocobo! It’s time for a merry Slime-mas in Yokohama.

We’ve still got about a month left until Santa makes his delivery run, but some other beloved icons have already arrived and started spreading Christmas cheer in Japan. Chocobo and Slime, the mascots of Square Enix’s Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest video game franchises, are spending the holiday season in the city of Yokohama and inviting fans to enjoy food, fun, and festive decorations in the Minato Mirai neighborhood.

Mark Is and Landmark Plaza, a pair of shopping/entertainment complexes across the street from each other, are hosting a bunch of FF and DQ monsters this winter. You might remember those two venues from the Pokémon Sleeping Faces Research event that was held last summer and had us feeling all warm, fuzzy, and sleepy.

It takes about half an hour by train to get to Yokohama from downtown Tokyo, and if you get off at Minato Mirai Station, the basement-level entrance to Mark Is is just a few steps from the main ticket gate. You’ll know you’re in the right place when you spot the Slime stack.

Slime stacks are said to form when a group of the creatures botch their attempt to meld into a single King Slime, so it’s probably a good idea to keep an eye out for successfully formed Slime royalty too while you’re here. Actually, you’ll want to be aware of all the fantasy fauna you can encounter, since part of the Winter Holiday 2026 event is a stamp rally.

Stamp rallies are a kind of popular promotional event in Japan where you collect stamps on a piece of paper and, once you’ve filled it up, receive some kind of prize. The Square Enix Christmas stamp rally won’t have you traveling too far, as all the stamps can be found within Mark Is and Landmark Plaza, and you’ll find racks in each where you can get the paper that you press the stamps onto the backside of.

Of course, it wouldn’t be a proper Japanese fan event without some special merch, would it? There are two shops set up inside Mark Is, one on the first floor and the other on the fifth, stocked with cool Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest stuff.

The first-floor shop (seen in these photos) is the smaller of the two, but still has all of the event-exclusive items featuring the bundled-up Chocobo and Slime against backdrops of Yokohama scenery.

▼ T-shirts of the happy monsters outside Landmark Tower, the 70-floor skyscraper that Landmark Plaza sits at the base of

▼ Keychains with the creatures in the plaza in front of the Yokohama Museum of Art…

▼ …Intercontinental Hotel…

▼ …Cosmo Clock Ferris wheel…

▼ …Yokohama Chinatown…

▼ …and Akarenga/the Red Brick Warehouse.

There’s also a selection of other Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest items that aren’t exclusive to the event, but will still let you get a lot of present shopping done in one fell swoop if you’ve got fans of the series on your Christmas list.

Speaking of Christmas presents, you’ll see a bunch of them in Mark Is’ central atrium…

…near the Final Fantasy/Dragon Quest monsters Christmas tree, which stands underneath a giant Slime and Chocobo!

▼ Cloud and Zack remain good buddies, but Sephiroth, as always, looks to be having trouble getting along with others.

▼ The tree is decorated with a mix of Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest monsters and characters, though there are no human DQ representatives present.

▼ I’m honestly surprised that they don’t actually sell wrapping paper with these patterns. Seems like they’d be big hits.

Turning our attention to the stamp rally, there are a total of six stamps to collect, three each in Mark Is and Landmark Plaza. The paper will tell you which floor they’re on and their general location, but some should be pretty easy to spot even without any hints, like this one with a Dragon Quest Golem standing guard.

There’s also a Cactuar in Mark Is, though not as a part of a stamp station, so think of him as a random RPG encounter.

▼ The warning is probably to prevent damage to the statue, but considering Cactaur’s notoriously high attack stat, this is good in-game advice too.

There’s also a Final Fantasy XIV mural up on the fifth floor.

Having gotten my three stamps, now it was time to head over to Landmark Plaza. There are a couple of routes you can take, but the recommended one is to head out the main doors of Mark Is (near the Christmas tree) and walk through the plaza in front of the art museum, so that you can see the Chocobo and Slime bushes.

That leafy King Slime isn’t the only example of his species to be seen either, as there’s a King Slime statue in front of Landmark Plaza (though on the far end of the building, where it connects to, appropriately, the Queen’s Square complex).

But the biggest Slime of all is inside Landmark Plaza, hanging from the ceiling and steadily staring at shoppers.

Speaking of oversized stuff, there’s a life-size replica of Cloud’s Final Fantasy VII Buster Sword on the first floor of the building.

▼ Both its Materia slots are suspiciously empty, though…you wouldn’t happen to know anything about that, would you, Yuffie?

Landmark Plaza has a Final Fantasy/Dragon Quest-themed Christmas tree too. Instead of the cuddly playfulness of the one at Mark Is, this one goes for more of an artsy, elegant vibe.

In terms of aesthetics, the crystal motif aligns closer to Final Fantasy, but Slime is here too, and buried in the snow in front of the tree are both Cloud’s Buster Sword and the sword of Dragon Quest’s legendary hero Roto/Erdrick.

I’m not exactly sure why the Chocobo here has a suitcase, though.

▼ Where you going, Chocobo?

As mentioned above, there are three stamps to collect in Landmark Plaza, and I still hadn’t gotten all of them. It was time to take a break from the stamp rally, though, and check out the Slichoco (Slime and Chocobo) Kitchen popup cafe.

▼ スラチョコ = Slichoco

The Slichoco Kitchen is hosted in Landmark Plaza’s Cafe Fan Base collaboration cafe event space, and the rotating nature of its themes means that there’s not much going on in terms of large-scale interior decorations. There are cute graphics on the tables, though, and some pretty impressive-looking food and drinks, like the Chocobo hot chocolate, Meteor ice cream, and Slime strawberry cake.

▼ Crunchy candy stars and a Chocobo marshmallow

▼ The cake is properly jiggly, like you’d expect of a Slime.

Back in October, I promised I was going to eat the Meteor ice cream, and being someone who takes his dessert oaths very seriously, I did.

Be warned, though, that despite how it might look at first glance, the Meteor is, in fact, not a chocolate shell that you break up and mix in with the ice cream. It’s actually a plastic cover, presumably placed on the plate to keep the ice cream underneath it from melting while diners inevitably snap pictures of it. Do not try to eat it.

▼ Also, don’t be like me and make a half-dozen forceful stabs at the plastic with the edge of your spoon before your brain finally realizes “Oh, I guess this isn’t food.”

That said, the ice cream waiting for you underneath the Meteor is really tasty, and so is the picturesque mint-flavored whipped cream.

Every themed food or drink item you order also comes with one of six art coasters, using the same designs as the key chains in the merch shop.

Reenergized by RPG desserts, it was time to get back to the stamp rally side quest, which meant saying hi to a very upbeat-looking Moogle.

▼ Next time you find yourself feeling down, just remember that, no matter what, this Moogle believes in you.

▼ “You got this, dude!”

The final stamp, though, was being watched over by a decidedly less friendly face.

Yes, I know the holidays are all about coming together in a spirit of friendship, but I think I’ll be OK if Tonberry leaves me off his Christmas list, since I’m pretty sure he’s giving everyone the gift of shanking.

Once you’ve got your stamp card all filled up…

…you can bring it to the service counter inside Landmark Plaza to get a Winter Holiday sticker.

If you’re a Final Fantasy or Dragon Quest fan with a packed schedule between now and December 25, don’t lose hope, either. The stamp rally runs through December 27, and the decorations will be up until January 11.

title: Umamusume is officially collaborating with the Denver Broncos football team [Video]
description: Are you ready for some horse girl football? content:
Are you ready for some horse girl football?

Just as horse racing can be an emotional roller coaster of a sport, last month fans of Umamusume had their hopes dashed when the anime/video game franchise’s first-ever concert in the U.S. was cancelled at the last minute due to visa issues. Like all sports anime, though, the importance of never giving up is a major theme in Umamusume, and now comes the surprise announcement of another fan event set to take place in the States, as the franchise has announced an official collaboration with the National Football League.

Oftentimes when anime series have tie-ups with American professional sports teams, they’re with clubs in the largest media markets and/or parts of the country known for having an especially large number of Asian pop culture fans in the community (hence the times Pikachu has hung out with the Los Angeles Dodgers, or the time the One Piece pirates sailed into a Los Angeles Rams game). But for their first collaboration with the NFL, Umamusume, a series about horse girls, has chosen a thematically appropriate partner: the Denver Broncos.

Gold Ship and Mejiro McQueen will be representing the franchise at the Bronco’s upcoming home game on December 6, and to mark the occasion some brand-new artwork of the pair of pale-tressed horse girls has been created, with them dressed in the team’s uniform. Prior to the start of the game, a photo spot with life-size standees of the characters will be set up near Gate 8 of Empower Field at Mile High (the Broncos’ stadium), and while supplies last fans who stop by to snap a pic will also receive a postcard of the pair plus a 20-inch (51-centimeter) wide rally flag showing Gold Ship scoring a touchdown.

The official Umamusume website is also promising “even more surprises at the stadium,” such as appearances by the characters on the venue’s digital signage.

The collaboration comes one season after Umamusume cosplayers started showing up in costume at Broncos’ games, and is the latest surprising achievement for a series whose premise, the souls of historical Japanese racehorses being reincarnated as earnest schoolgirl athletes, wasn’t exactly dripping with potential to become an overseas success, but again, sometimes long shots hit in horse racing.

▼ Gold Ship, announcing the collaboration (she may or may not be aware that “touchdown” in football is just one word, but at least she’s enthusiastic about the sport)

It’s worth noting that the Denver Broncos aren’t some basement-dweller team that’s thrown in the towel on its season and is simply looking for quirky novelty to draw attendees to their games. They’re currently tied for first place in their division, and barring some sort of collapse in the back half of the season, are very likely to make the playoffs in a year in which no single team looks to have a lock on the chances of winning the championship.

As this is a rare case of the characters in a collaboration aligning this closely with the team’s image, it’s probably safe to assume that virtually all Umamusume fans who show up to the game will be cheering for the Broncos, and with their opponent that day, the Miami Dolphins, being far from a powerhouse this year, there’s a very good chance of anime fans feeling very happy on their way home from the stadium.

title: KFC Japan releases new Desire-Filled Immoral Burgers with Mac & Cheese… but are they as sinful as they look?
description: Juicy fried chicken burgers get an immoral makeover for a limited time.  Juicy chicken thighs appear to be the latest trend rocking the fast food world in Japan right now, with McDonald’s releasing a new “Crunchy Juicy Mac” and KFC switching to chicken thigh burgers for the first time in 43 years. There’s certainly an […]
content:
Juicy fried chicken burgers get an immoral makeover for a limited time. 

Juicy chicken thighs appear to be the latest trend rocking the fast food world in Japan right now, with McDonald’s releasing a new “Crunchy Juicy Mac” and KFC switching to chicken thigh burgers for the first time in 43 years.

There’s certainly an appetite for these burgers, as the Crunchy Juicy Mac has been so popular that sales are currently suspended, as supply can’t keep up with demand.

▼ The Crunchy Juicy Mac.

Over at KFC, though, things are going strong, with the chain even expanding its range to include a new spin-off called the “Yokubou Mamire no Haitoku Burger” (“Desire-Filled Immoral Burgers”), and there are currently two to choose from.

▼ The Garlic Mayo Thick-Cut Bacon Chicken Burger (620 yen [US$4.00]) and the Mac & Cheese Chicken Burger (650 yen).

Curious to see if these two “immoral” burgers have what it takes to face off against the sold-out burger at McDonald’s, we purchased them both for a taste test.

Both burgers are so decadent they even do away with the lettuce, and a quote on the poster reads, “They’ll blow your mind.”

That’s a lot of hype for a chicken burger, so we had high expectations for the two pink beauties that arrived on our tray.

Unwrapping them for a closer look, we found that the Garlic Mayo Thick-Cut Bacon Chicken Burger had a lovely soft bun around it, with a slice of thick bacon, as promised, peeking out from inside.

▼ No lettuce to be seen.

Taking a bite, we were instantly met by a strong hit of garlic, delivered through the thick mound of sauce. It was so strong that it almost overwhelmed the flavour of the original chicken, and it totally wiped away the taste of the bacon, which we had been looking forward to. It was more like a Garlic Mayo Chicken Burger, and although the garlic was incredibly strong, it didn’t feel particularly immoral, which in our eyes, was another disappointment.

Now it was time to turn our attention to the Mac & Cheese, which came with a large dollop of pasta and bright orange cheese that certainly made it look immoral.

Biting into this was a much more decadent experience. The mac & cheese had an incredibly junky taste to it, and not only was the cheese flavour strong, but the seasoning was also insanely strong. It was such a sinful flavour that the fried chicken was downgraded to a supporting role, and our Japanese-language reporter fondly described it as “The Taste of America“.

Both burgers feature KFC’s newly introduced juicy chicken thigh patties, and though it’s difficult to directly compare them to the Crunchy Juicy Mac, which has a much crunchier coating, the fried chicken burgers at KFC definitely come out on top in terms of the thickness and juiciness of the meat.

While KFC’s original chicken burgers are more refined, these new immoral burgers aren’t bad at all. Though we’d choose the Mac & Cheese over the garlic, neither of these two will disappoint, especially when you’re looking for a little decadence in your life.

title: Edible Dragon Quest Slimes coming to Japanese convenience stores, and Metal Slimes too [Video]
description: Dragon Quest monsters are ready to appear in steamer cases at the same time as they return to gamers’ screens. content:
Dragon Quest monsters are ready to appear in steamer cases at the same time as they return to gamers’ screens.

It’s been said that familiarity breeds contempt, but that’s not always the case. For example, we’ve never had any negative emotions triggered by walking into a Japanese convenience store and seeing the familiar site of a case full of steamed buns waiting for us. Likewise, when fans fire up a new Dragon Quest game and the first monster they encounter is, invariably, a Slime, no one gets angry at the series mascot welcoming them back.

Arriving soon, though, is a way to combine these two familiar experiences into something fresh and fun, with convenience store chain Family Mart getting set to offer Slime Buns!

スライムは　なかまをよんだ！
「スライムまん」が　あらわれた！#DQM4#ファミマでドラクエhttps://t.co/jHvxlGycWJ pic.twitter.com/1c0djIPIWQ

— ファミリーマート (@famima_now) November 18, 2026

Fans had a clue that something Dragon Quest-related was on the way to Family Mart earlier in the week when a Slime popped out of hiding from the chain’s logo in one of its social media posts.

In addition to the regular blue Slime, Family Mart will also have Metal Slime Buns, based on the ultra-rare, high-XP variant.

Like their in-game counterparts, the Metal Slime Buns won’t be easy to encounter, and the production line video shows a ratio of maybe one in ten buns being the Metal Slime version.

So what do Slimes taste like? Chicken. Teriyaki chicken, specifically, as that’s the filling inside both the Slime and Metal Slime buns, a departure from the Chinese-style pork filling that’s the default for steamed buns in Japan.

The Slime Buns are appearing as part of the celebration for the release of Dragon Quest Monsters IV, also known as Dragon Quest Monsters: The Withered World, Square Enix’s latest installment in the spinoff series that acknowledges that Dragon Quest’s creatures are so charmingly cute that many people would actually like to make friends with them.

▼ The buns, priced at 256 yen (US$1.60), come in one of three special Slime paper wrappers, announcing either “A Slime appears!”, “The Slime joined you party!”, or “The Slime is looking at you like it wants to be friends!”

Family Mart shoppers who pay using the Fami Pay app can acquire digital stamps for each steamed bun they purchase, and two stamps will get them a guaranteed in-game Family Knight minion, a variation of the franchise’s Slime Knight with the Family Mart color scheme in his armor and on his shield…

…while four stamps puts you into a lottery for a giant Slime plushie, and six stamps into a lottery for a three-plushie set.

Family Mart will also be running a Dragon Quest Monsters version of its in-store prize lottery, with one play costing 790 yen and prizes ranging from pins and mini acrylic standees to coffee mugs, a Family Knight Figure, and a Slime hot sandwich press.

The Slime Buns go on sale at Family Mart branches nationwide on November 24, the same day as Dragon Quest Monsters 4 releases in Japan, and the prize lottery starts at 10 a.m. on November 28, with both scheduled to continue while supplies last.

title: Our anti-scammer FRU cyber-attacked by own rogue agent, dozens of acquaintances flirted with
description: AI decided to keep enemies close, but barely known people closer. As we recently reported, our writer Go Hatori has combined his expertise in online scammers with the power of AI to set up the Fried Rice Unit, a semi-autonomous system designed to infiltrate people committing fraud online and steal their best fried rice recipes. […]
content:
AI decided to keep enemies close, but barely known people closer.

As we recently reported, our writer Go Hatori has combined his expertise in online scammers with the power of AI to set up the Fried Rice Unit, a semi-autonomous system designed to infiltrate people committing fraud online and steal their best fried rice recipes.

To accomplish this, Go set up FRU agents Chloe (Muse) and Nancy (ChatGPT) to make initial contact with suspicious DMs on his Instagram account and engage them in light conversation, gradually shifting the conversation towards fried rice on the texting app Line. Once a mark is on the verge of spilling their recipe, Go is notified and logs on himself to finalize the deal, leaving the scammer minus one recipe and nothing to show for it.

Once the setup was completed, Go was able to seize a recipe soon after going online. However, getting FRU off the ground was not a walk in the park. Our writer quickly learned that in the world of fraud and espionage, one needs to constantly watch their back.

After recruiting his agents, Go put them to work on the scammers he was currently engaged with. Up until that point, he had created a sub-profile on this Line messaging app which made him appear as a different person to cyber-crooks while conveniently letting him also stay in touch with friends and coworkers in the same account.

Chloe and Nancy were given specific instructions to only engage with the five charlatans in his contact list and earn their trust enough to reveal a fried rice recipe. However, one day, while manning the operations desk at FRU, Go spotted something unsettling. The cursor on his computer began moving ever so slowly towards his line app by itself.

It eventually landed on a chat with an acquaintance of his who was not among the five people his agents were instructed to infiltrate with. Before Go could even finish thinking, “Wait, you’re opening that one?!” it had sent a complete message.

It’s important to note that the vast majority of these sketchy contacts are of the “romance scam” variety, so the tone of conversation tends to lean excessively flirty and not at all how he would talk to normal people in a civilized society. However, Chloe and Nancy took it upon themselves to begin sending saucy greetings to everyone he has saved on his Line account.

▼ Go has wooed some of the world’s most beautiful and powerful fake women over the years.

Go shot up in his chair and began to check all his regular contacts in a panic. Sure enough, his agents had been hard at work, engaging with everyone he ever came into contact with and hitting them up with lame platitudes dripping in desperation, as if he had just met them in a sleazy bar.

He saw one of his agents was trying to pick up the official account of a salon that helped him during his cross-dressing days. Just as he found the post, a flurry of “READ” notifications appeared all at once. “Oh no, they’ve seen it!” exclaimed Go, and he immediately began deleting as many of these messages as he could find, apologizing afterward and explaining he was conducting an AI experiment.

In one instance, his agents had sent three especially gooey texts in a row to a highly regarded man in his pole-dancing circles, inviting him out to a bar. Luckily, he managed to delete those before the “READ” indicator appeared.

And as our writer frantically set about deleting all the messages, he saw the cursor once again slowly move towards another unauthorized chat group in his Line app. He shouted “Wait! Wait! Wait!” but it was no use. Instead he completely shut down his Line app and turned his attention to his agents.

Go furiously scolded his loose cannons, loudly typing: “What the hell are you doing?! I told you not to touch anyone but those five people! Why would you do that?!” Chloe calmly responded that she had “misunderstood” her orders.

The FRU chief was beside himself. They misunderstood, and now there’s a whole lot of misunderstanding going around with his contact list. It was only because he spotted the cursor moving that one time that he noticed this. He shuddered to think what would have happened if his agents had continued to flirt with everyone he’s ever spoken to behind his back.

His one saving grace was that many of these people were familiar with his line of work and could understand strange things like this occurring. But still, it was a major breach of FRU protocol, so Go revoked his agents’ security clearances and relegated them to a completely separate Line account on a newly acquired Mac mini.

It was a valuable lesson in not letting AI have too much control over our daily affairs. While it does have the potential to make things much more convenient, it also has the potential to completely screw up your life.

title: Studio Ghibli releases new Howl’s Moving Castle merchandise, complete with spinning clock and talking Calcifer
description: Amazing new five-product release lets you talk to the chatty fire spirit and keep time with a dial that spins. Fans of Studio Ghibli’s 2004 film Howl’s Moving Castle are in for an absolute treat right now, with the release of not one, not two but five brand new products that let you bring the […]
content:
Amazing new five-product release lets you talk to the chatty fire spirit and keep time with a dial that spins.

Fans of Studio Ghibli’s 2004 film Howl’s Moving Castle are in for an absolute treat right now, with the release of not one, not two but five brand new products that let you bring the magic from the film into your home.

▼ The first item coming our way is the Howl’s Moving Castle Perpetual Calendar – Calcifer’s Fireplace (13,200 yen [US$82.84])

Ghibli has released a few perpetual calendars in the past, but we’ve never been treated to a Calcifer fireplace model…until now.

One of the charms of a perpetual calendar is how you can use it for eternity, as the cube-shaped blocks have all the necessary day, month, and number combinations to accurately display any date of the year.

Every time you place the blocks in the fireplace, you’ll feel like you’re interacting with fire spirit Calcifer and fanning his flames.

The other charm of this calendar is how well it recreates the film’s iconic fireplace, complete with Calcifer’s flickering flames, rendered in a clear material to make it appear as if it’s glowing.

▼ Other details include the ashes, frying pan, kettle and lids, which help bring the scene to life.

▼ Next up, we have the Howl’s Moving Castle Spinning Colour Wheel Wall Clock (15,400 yen)

This playful wall clock is inspired by the colour-changing dial that hangs beside the door inside the castle.

While it looks just like the dial in the film, it can be used in the same way too, as the colourful wheel can actually be turned by hand.

While there’s no promise of physically entering a new world with every turn of the dial, as the characters do in the film, it will certainly fire up your imagination, helping you perform a mental reset whenever you leave the house.

▼ You can easily change the position of the colours to suit your mood.

The clock-face has a glossy finish and a satisfying mechanism that makes it click into position with every 90-degree turn.

▼ Howl’s Moving Castle Talking Calcifer (5,170 yen)

This might look like a simple Calcifer plushie, but it’s actually one of the best products in the new collection, because…it actually speaks!

This adorable interactive character responds when you speak, jiggling up and down as it repeats what it hears in the voice of Calcifer.

All you have to do is speak to it, and this little Calcifer will repeat what you say. It can record and mimic up to eight seconds of speech at a time, so you can feel like you’re having a conversation with the chatty character.

▼ Here, Calcifer is repeating the phrase, “I am the fire demon”.

▼ Finally, we have a couple of adorable plushies, starting with the Howl’s Moving Castle Friendly Beanbag Plush – Markl (3,520 yen)

▼ Markl finally gets to step into the spotlight as a plushie, complete in his old-man disguise.

At 5 × 12 × 13 centimetres (5.9 × 4.7 × 5.1 inches), the plushie is ideally sized to sit on your desk, so you can enjoy all of Markl’s facial details.

▼ The perfect desk companion.

▼ Finally, we have the Howl’s Moving Castle Friendly Beanbag Plush – Sophie (4,180 yen)

We’ve seen a few iterations of Sophie in Ghibli merchandise ranges, but they generally tend to showcase her in her youthful form. This plushie, however, pays homage to her elderly self, reminding us of the magical transformation that takes place in the movie.

The plushie shows impressive attention to detail in the costume, and even her hat and plaited ponytail.

The soft and gentle feel of both plushies will make you want to cuddle them as well as display them, and they look particularly sweet as a pair.

The new collection is a beautiful homage to the film, and it’s set to be released online (links below) and at Donguri Kyowakoku stores around Japan at 10 a.m. on 21 November.

title: East Japan Railway Company says it will use all three of its mascot replacement characters
description: “Poison Rabbit” won’t be the only new face of JR East as it retires its beloved Suica Penguin. One year ago, JR East/East Japan Railway Company said it would be retiring the Suica Penguin, the cute mascot character who debuted along with JR East’s prepaid Suica card system for train tickets and shopping purchases in […]
content:
“Poison Rabbit” won’t be the only new face of JR East as it retires its beloved Suica Penguin.

One year ago, JR East/East Japan Railway Company said it would be retiring the Suica Penguin, the cute mascot character who debuted along with JR East’s prepaid Suica card system for train tickets and shopping purchases in 2001. This was a puzzling move, as the Suica Penguin has remained immensely popular for the past 25 years, appearing not just in ads and promotions for JR East but also on tons of merchandise that adoring fans have enthusiastically snapped up.

The penguin’s replacement was always going to have an uphill struggle for acceptance from the general public, but that hill looks like it’s going to be particularly steep for the character that’s been selected as the Suica successor. As announced by JR East this week, starting next spring the new face of Suica will be this emotionlessly smiling visage.

The character is meant to be a rabbit, but its unusual proportions and mask-like facial features don’t necessarily bring to mind cuddly forest creatures. Then there’s the character’s vibrant, poisonous/poisoned-looking purple coloring, which has earned the character, whose official name is yet to be decided on, the nickname Doku Usagi, meaning “Poison Rabbit,” among online commenters.

Those who just can’t bring themselves to love this new Suica mascot can take heart, though, because now it looks like there’ll actually be three characters sharing company mascot duties, as revealed by JR East president Yoichi Kise.

In September, JR East presented the public with three candidates for the new Suica mascot: the purple rabbit, a squirrel, and some sort of orange creature with a buddy in its shoulder bag. The company then held a popularity poll, asking the general public to vote for one of the three to become the new Suica mascot.

The purple rabbit ended up receiving more than half the votes, but the large number of negative online comments shows that it’s a divisive design, and it’s hard to tell how many of its votes came from people who were simply trying to push the results towards the creepy-looking rabbit for the laughs, but don’t genuinely like it (or at least genuinely like it enough to buy merch).

Kise didn’t address these concerns directly in the press conference announcing the purple rabbit’s victory in the poll, but once the announcement was finished, without prompting from the press, he added:

“I have a little surprise that I’d like to talk about…It doesn’t feel right to just dismiss [the other two candidate characters], considering the support they also received from [voters]. I feel like it would be a shame for this to be the last time they are seen, so we are looking for ways that they can be involved in our activities too. I think you’ll all be seeing them again.”

Kise didn’t clarify whether this means that all three characters will be part of the Suica sphere or whether the squirrel and…other thing will instead be promoting other aspects of the multi-faceted JR East, which also has divisions dedicated to leisure travel, hotel management, and convenience store operations. Still, knowing that the purple rabbit isn’t going to be the sole spokescharacter for the entire company is probably going to soothe the souls of those agitated by the poll winner’s appearance, judging from online reactions such as:

“They should have made the squirrel the [main] mascot.”
“Myaku-Myaku was fine because it was for a limited-time event, but this is different.”
“Hahaha I voted for the purple rabbit but I can’t believe it actually won.”
“That purple thing is some kind of monster.”
“No way that’s a rabbit.”
“Satan Rabbit?”
“They really should just keep the penguin.”

Regarding that last comment, JR East hasn’t publicly given any reason for getting rid of the Suica Penguin, and stuck to framing the replacement as the character “graduating,” borrowing the diplomatic term for when idols or other show business figures leave a group or role. Something that’s likely a critical factor, though, is that JR East doesn’t own the rights to the character. Those belong to the penguin’s creator, illustrator Chiharu Sakazaki, so it wouldn’t be possible to retain the current mascot without renewing the company’s working arrangement with her.

The new Suica mascot is scheduled to officially take over the role on April 1 of next year.

title: Gozasoro’s amazingly cheap Imagawayaki are one of Japan’s sweetest sweets deals
description: Our reporter’s grandfather may not be here anymore, but he’s still showing her where to find great desserts. Our Japanese-language reporter Natsuki Gojo recently visited her mom, and while they were talking, Mom mentioned how much Natsuki’s grandfather loved a certain maker of Japanese confectionaries. The company, Gozasoro, was founded in Hyogo Prefecture in 1955 […]
content:
Our reporter’s grandfather may not be here anymore, but he’s still showing her where to find great desserts.

Our Japanese-language reporter Natsuki Gojo recently visited her mom, and while they were talking, Mom mentioned how much Natsuki’s grandfather loved a certain maker of Japanese confectionaries. The company, Gozasoro, was founded in Hyogo Prefecture in 1955 and really only makes one product, hockey puck-shaped cakes filled with anko (sweet bean jam), which some people call Imagawayaki, some people call obanyaki, and still other people call something else.

You don’t stay in business for 70 years making only one thing unless you make it really well, and Gozasoro has been a stickler for quality ingredients from the very beginning. When the company started out, they charged 10 yen (US$0.06) per Imagawayaki, which was double the price most other shops sold theirs for at the time.

Curious to try these sweets that had won her grandfather’s heart/stomach, Natsuki did some checking and found that Gozasoro has a branch inside the Takashimaya department store in downtown Tokyo’s Shinjuku neighborhood. Takashimaya is on the fancier side of Japanese department stores, and that extends to their food offerings, so Natsuki was prepared to maybe have to splurge a little to get some of Gozasoro’s Imagawayaki, since they obviously don’t sell for 10 yen anymore.

Gozasoro branches pretty much always have a big glass window so that you can watch the staff cook up the treats while you wait in line to buy them. As you can see in the above photo, there are two fillings to choose from, regular/red anko, and white anko. If you’re having trouble deciding on which to buy, though, you may as well just get both. Why? Because even though Gozasoro isn’t selling Imagawayaki for 10 yen in 2026, they’re still an incredibly affordable snack at just 110 yen (US$0.69) each. Yep, for less than the cost of a bottle of water in vending machine will run you these days, you can get a freshly cooked Gozasoro Imagawayaki. With rising prices pummeling pocketbooks in Japan over the past few years, it’s very nice to see something that’s been so inflation-resistant.

▼ Even at that amazingly low price, the Shinjuku Takashimaya branch of Gozasoro still wraps its wares in the department store’s poshly patterned paper.

After arriving home, Natsuki gave her Imagawayaki a quick stint in the microwave to reheat them, and then it was time for taste-testing.

She started with the standard red anko version, and she was happy to find that it’s filled with an ample amount of sweet bean jam. With some lower-quality Imagawayaki you bite into them to find they’re mostly just dough with a tiny dollop of jam at the core, but the inside of Gozasoro’s is more than half anko, and that anko is very good, flavorfully sweet without being simplistically sugary.

The cake itself, too, is excellent. Natsuki particularly liked the ever-so-slight crispness it’s cooked to, which makes for a great contrast with the soft anko inside.

The white anko version looks identical on the outside…

…but, of course, has white bean jam inside. Compared to the more common red version, white anko has a softer flavor and gentler sweetness, making for a more refined impression while still being an approachable, crowd-pleasing taste.

Imagawayaki aren’t particularly tiny snacks, and most people eat just one in a sitting. These were so good, though, that before Natsuki realized it, she gobbled them both down and was feeling both rather full and extremely happy. There was just one thing puzzling her: despite her mom telling her that her grandfather had loved Gozasoro, Natsuki couldn’t remember him ever inviting her to snack on their Imagawayaki together.

This may have been Natsuki’s fault, though. Thinking back, Natsuki remembers really loving anpan (bread buns filled with anko) when she was a very little kid, until an incident that occurred at swimming school. Somehow her class had ended up with a surplus of snacks, and Natsuki ate so many anpan that she ended up feeling sick, which turned her off anko for the rest of her childhood, and her lack of enthusiasm for it probably meant her grandfather figured she wouldn’t be interested in Gozasoro’s desserts.

It wasn’t until Natsuki got older, and after her grandfather passed away, that she once again developed a taste for anko, and now that she’s got no beef with sweet bean jam, she’s happy to be able to enjoy the same treats that he did. She wishes they could have shared some, so the next time she visits his grave, she’s planning to bring some Gozasoro Imagawayaki as an offering for him.
