title: Japan’s beautiful new Pokémon hotel room gives you and Dragonite a place to take a break
description: Flying over to Fukui as part of your Japan trip? The prefecture’s Poké-bassador has a room all ready for you. Dragonite isn’t a Pokémon that likes to stay in one place very long. The Dragon/Flying Type is reportedly capable of circumnavigating the globe in just 16 hours, and it puts its wings to good use […]
content:
Flying over to Fukui as part of your Japan trip? The prefecture’s Poké-bassador has a room all ready for you.

Dragonite isn’t a Pokémon that likes to stay in one place very long. The Dragon/Flying Type is reportedly capable of circumnavigating the globe in just 16 hours, and it puts its wings to good use flying hither and yon.

Of course, even Dragonite needs a place to spend the night when it’s roaming far from home, and it’s got a very special place to do that with Japan’s new Traveling Dragonite hotel room.

You’ll find this unique offering in Fukui, the prefecture that Dragonite serves as tourism ambassador Pokémon for. Fukui is famous for the dinosaur fossils that have been excavated there, and with the Japanese word for dinosaur, kyoryu, translating literally as “terrifying dragon,” the draconic Dragonite was a natural choice to partner with the prefecture for the Pokémon Local Acts project, which seeks to shine a spotlight on beautiful and interesting parts of Japan that tourists might overlook if they’re only focusing on the largest cities and most famous sightseeing attractions.

The Traveling Dragonite Room is located on the 11th floor of Awara Onsen Grandia Housen, a hotel in the Fukui hot spring town of Awara. Within the room, which can accommodate up to six guests, what look to be hundreds of Dragonites are waiting to greet you, as the Pokémon serves as the muse for the room’s tapestries and woven fabric pillowcases, bed runners, and cushion covers, all of which were created by local Fukui artisans using traditional methods. There are also Dragonite plushies on the beds, and while not specifically mentioned in the press release, there’s a chance that they could be yours to take home with you when you check out.

The room consists of two sections, a bedroom area and a living room area, the latter with tatami reed flooring and a raised alcove in which more Dragonite artwork is displayed. As for why the room is on the 11th floor, it’s so that looking out the window at the expansive view of the nearby mountains and Sakai Plains will give you a perspective similar to what Dragonite would see on a Fukui flyover.

The room has its own shower and bathtub, but with Grandia Housen being a hot spring inn, you’ll also want to take time to check out its traditional communal onsen baths, including the open-air rooftop ones.

As you can see on the above map, Fukui is pretty far off the Tokyo-to-Osaka line that most visitors to Japan spend most of their time on. Getting off the so-called “golden route” can reward you with some still relatively hidden gems of the Japan travel scene, such as this lovely little town, this unusual workshop, or this very tasty meal, all of which we found in Fukui, and combining them with a night in a Dragonite-themed hotel room would make the whole side trip even better.

Reservations are open now for the special Pokémon room through the Grandia Housen website, with the earliest available stays coming up soon on November 29.

title: Life-size Gundam statue’s head returning to Tokyo neighborhood this month
description: Odaiba welcomes back the head of the RX-0 Unicorn Gundam. East Japan is suffering from a serious shortage of life-size Gundams these days. Yokohama’s full-scale statue of the original RX-78 Gundam has been gone since the spring of 2024, when it was moved to Osaka for the Expo 2025 world’s fair (and which was dismantled […]
content:
Odaiba welcomes back the head of the RX-0 Unicorn Gundam.

East Japan is suffering from a serious shortage of life-size Gundams these days. Yokohama’s full-scale statue of the original RX-78 Gundam has been gone since the spring of 2024, when it was moved to Osaka for the Expo 2025 world’s fair (and which was dismantled after that event ended), and Tokyo’s 1:1 recreation of the Unicorn Gundam, which had been greeting visitors from around the world in the city’s Odaiba neighborhood since 2017, was taken down at the end of this past August.

After anime’s most famous mecha series having some kind of large-scale presence in the Tokyo area for so long, for fans it definitely feels like there’s something missing now. Thankfully, while it’s still uncertain if or when Tokyo will be getting a new Gundam, statue, at least part of the Unicorn Gundam is coming back, as the life-size head unit will soon return to Odaiba for public display.

Starting this weekend, the head of the RX-0 Unicorn Gundam will once again be back in the Festival Plaza outside the Diver City shopping/entertainment complex, just a short walk from Tokyo Teleport Station on the Rinkai Line or Daiba Station on the Yurikamome Line. While it will no longer sit at the top of the 19.7-meter (64.6-foot) tall robot like it used to, this new display will give fans a chance to see the head up-close and appreciate all the little details to its design, something that’ll be much easier to do at eye level than gazing up at it from far below like you used to have to.

Famously, the Unicorn Gundam’s head unit can reconfigure itself, having a single unicorn-like horn in its “Unicorn Mode” and a more traditional split forehead crest in its “Destroy Mode.” This feature was replicated in the life-size statue, as shown in the video below, but it’s unclear if the head will be switching modes while on display by itself.

This might not be the only Unicorn component that we’ll be seeing on display in the near future, either. “Right now, we can only display pieces,” says life-size Gundam project producer Kaori Shida, “so I’d like to at least have [them] hold something, move [their] position, or give [them] some kind of job to do.” It’s also too early to give up hope of ever seeing another Gundam Statue in east Japan. “Personally, I’d like to try a full remake of the original [RX-78 Gundam],” muses Masaki Kawahara, creative director of the Gundam Global Challenge initiative, “I think it would look cool if the maintenance hatch fully opened to reveal the inside, and then closed again to start the sequence.”

The Unicorn Gundam head will be on display from November 21, and is listed as being for a limited, although currently unspecified, time. Meanwhile, the head of the life-size RX-78 is scheduled to go on display in Osaka in early December, and for those in west Japan who want to see a life-size Gundam still standing tall, Fukuoka still has its Nu Gundam.
